articles.title: An AWS library stored SQS payloads in S3 without encryption for 4 years and nobody's tooling caught it
articles.excerpt: ✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading. In June 2016, a user reported about the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library. It is an official AWS library that stored large SQS mess…
articles.body: ✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading. In June 2016, a user reported about the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library. It is an official AWS library that stored large SQS message payloads in S3 without server-side encryption. The question: "the messages stored in S3 do not have encryption turned on. For the best HIPAA compliance, I think they should be?" The issue sat open for 4 years . It was resolved in July 2020 with version 1.1.0, which added SSE-KMS support. Why this matters The SQS Extended Client Library is used when message payloads exceed the 256KB SQS limit. The library transparently stores the payload in S3 and sends a pointer via SQS. The consuming application retrieves the payload from S3.

articles.body: I'm building Inquir Compute , a cloud platform for apps, databases, and background jobs. The kind of setup I have in mind is pretty common: an API, PostgreSQL, and maybe a worker. I can put those on a VPS, but then I'm also setting up HTTPS, collecting logs, and maintaining deployment scripts. For a small project, I'd rather spend that time on the app. Inquir lets you deploy from a GitHub repository, a Dockerfile, or an existing container image. The app can stay a regular HTTP server. You don't have to rewrite it around a platform-specific handler. Here's how deployment works with a small Node.js app. We'll deploy it, check a second version on a preview URL, and then roll back. articles.title: A Feature Isn't Finished Until the Player Can Read It
articles.excerpt: A mechanic can work exactly as coded and still be unclear to the person playing. That is an easy gap to miss while building a game. You know what each meter means. You know why an enemy changed direct…
articles.body: A mechanic can work exactly as coded and still be unclear to the person playing. That is an easy gap to miss while building a game. You know what each meter means. You know why an enemy changed direction. You know what a warning is supposed to tell the player. After spending time with the system, its logic starts to feel obvious. The player does not have that context. They see a screen, make a guess, and learn from what happens next. When I work on a small arcade shooter, I try to think about a mechanic in two parts: what the system does, and what the player can understand about it. A near miss can reward careful movement. A focus meter can give a player a reason to keep a streak alive. A risk indicator can make a powerful choice feel costly.

articles.title: A Completeness Gate Is Only as Complete as Its Required Set. Don't Let the Model Write It.
articles.excerpt: A completeness gate has two different problems: determining what must exist, and determining whether it exists. We keep treating them as one. One common design hands both to the same model. A generate…
articles.body: A completeness gate has two different problems: determining what must exist, and determining whether it exists. We keep treating them as one. One common design hands both to the same model. A generated change plan, policy bundle or control mapping goes in, the model is asked whether anything required is missing, and it answers against its own idea of what "required" means. If it reports nothing missing, the gate passes. Nothing alerts, because nothing failed. The check ran correctly against a list that was already short. Every Completeness Gate Solves Two Problems The first problem is enumeration: which elements must be present? The second is comparison: is each of them present in this artifact?

articles.excerpt: vCluster runs a full Kubernetes control plane as a pod inside a namespace of a host cluster. We use it to run our tenants' clusters: each one gets cluster-admin inside a real API boundary, without the…
articles.body: vCluster runs a full Kubernetes control plane as a pod inside a namespace of a host cluster. We use it to run our tenants' clusters: each one gets cluster-admin inside a real API boundary, without the cost of a dedicated cluster underneath. Anything self-contained inside the virtual cluster works out of the box: Deployments, Services, the operators a tenant installs. The trouble starts when a tenant writes an Argo CD Application that only the central Argo CD on the host can reconcile, an HTTPRoute that needs to attach to a shared Gateway, or an alert rule that belongs on the host ruler. Every multi-tenant platform grows these crossings: objects written on one side of a boundary that a controller on the other side has to act on.

articles.body: TL;DR Google says domestic flights have historically been cheapest around 39 days before departure, while international fares hit their lowest around 89 days out. The idea that Tuesday is the best day to book is largely a myth, with the cheapest booking day saving only about 1.4% versus the most expensive. Changing when and how you fly matters more: weekday travel can save up to 20% domestically, while nonstop flights cost around 20% more than connecting options. Booking a flight can sometimes feel like a gamble. You find a fare that looks reasonable, but instead of booking it, you start wondering whether it’ll be cheaper tomorrow. But wait too long, and you could end up paying even more.

articles.title: 31 Years Later, One of the Most Disturbing Thrillers Ever Made Is Officially Free on Streaming
articles.excerpt: Forget the Eli Roth movie, this 1995 horror movie belongs in the pantheon of so-bad-it's-good classics.
articles.body: Released in 1995, Ice Cream Man is the type of so-bad-it's-good horror movie that rarely gets made in the post- Get Out era where the genre is taken much more seriously. Directed by pornographer Paul Norman, who hoped this was his pivot to kid-friendly horror flicks, Ice Cream Man is a movie where a deranged killer mixes up bugs, human remains, and ice cream and feeds it to children. It's also a movie that spends a remarkable amount of time showing us what shoes everyone is wearing, as per a sponsorship agreement with Converse that probably cost some poor sneaker executive his job. Norman may have wanted to escape X-rated film, but he wound up making one of the creepiest stories ever put on film.

articles.body: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype , steered by zealots , inescapable . The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now. On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast.
